summary: Linda sits on the flat Sacramento Valley floor just north of the Yuba City–Marysville metro area, and the number that jumps out first is a home-price-to-income ratio under 5:1 — remarkably low for anywhere in California, where double-digit ratios are routine in coastal metros. At a median home value of $337,700 against $69,161 in household income, ownership math here looks plausible without dual six-figure salaries, though a 21.8% poverty rate signals that the local economy, anchored largely by agriculture, logistics, and public-sector jobs tied to nearby Beale Air Force Base, distributes that affordability unevenly. The landscape is unmistakably valley: wide-open sky, rice fields and orchards stretching to the Sutter Buttes — the world's smallest mountain range — visible on the eastern horizon, and summer highs that routinely push well past the 77°F annual average into triple digits from June through September. With 9.2 hours of daily sunshine year-round, shade and air conditioning are infrastructure, not amenities. The area is car-dependent and census-designated rather than incorporated, meaning no city government shapes its own zoning or parks budget. Linda is a place where California housing math finally pencils out, and the asterisk is everything that makes coastal California expensive in the first place — proximity, job density, and walkable infrastructure — is largely absent.
